target_customer: Small teams and developers who wanted to build web pages and prototypes without hiring a designer
problem: Design tools had not kept up with the web, so teams used desktop software like Photoshop and then hand coded the result.
business_model: Freemium SaaS with three paid tiers from about 10 to 50 dollars per month
product_category: Browser based visual web design tool

founders.name: Matt Colyer
founders.background_notes: TechCrunch says he and Ben Ogle met as engineers at AdRoll.

founders.name: Ben Ogle
founders.background_notes: Met Matt Colyer as an engineer at AdRoll per TechCrunch.

exit.reason: Team joined GitHub; product shut down on 2014-10-31, about eight months later.

competitors.name: Adobe Photoshop and desktop design software
competitors.what: Offline design tools the product aimed to replace for web layouts
competitors.traction_then: TechCrunch called Easel less robust than offline software

competitors.name: Divshot
competitors.what: Hosted editor for manual code based prototyping, named in Easel's own comparison listing

technical_complexity.rationale: Real time multi user editing, a drag and drop editor, an HTML and CSS importer through a Chrome extension and clean exports were hard for two engineers in 2012.

defensibility.rationale: No data or network moat; a feature set that Webflow and Adobe tools could and did match.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: GitHub acquired the team in Jan 2014 and shut the product down by 31 Oct 2014.

market_need_then: TechCrunch in Aug 2012 framed demand as teams wanting ideas online without a designer; no traction numbers were reported.

branding.domain_note: Used easel.io, a .io domain rather than the .com.
branding.community_and_virality: A Show HN post in June 2012 preceded launch coverage; no merch or fan community found.

brand_strength.rationale: Pleasant name tied to design, but no brand coverage was found and it had little time or traction.

outcome_analysis: Easel launched out of YC in Aug 2012 as a collaborative browser based web design tool, was acquired by GitHub in Jan 2014 with terms undisclosed, and was shut down on 31 Oct 2014 after new signups halted. The pattern fits a team acquisition rather than a product outcome. No funding beyond YC was found and no traction numbers were published.
